sources.title: William Fulton, Algebraic Curves: An Introduction to Algebraic Geometry (2008 electronic edition; Internet Archive snapshot of the author-hosted PDF)
sources.locator: Ch. 3 §§3.1-3.3 (printed pp. 31-41: multiple points and tangent lines, multiplicities and local rings, intersection numbers including the full uniqueness and existence proof of Theorem 3 and the Lemma in the proof of property (5)) and Ch. 5 §§5.1-5.6 (printed pp. 53-66: definitions, linear systems, Bezout's theorem with its proof and corollaries, multiple points, Max Noether's theorem and applications)

read_evidence.method: Full 129-page PDF (706,612 bytes) downloaded from the Internet Archive snapshot of the author's CurveBook.pdf, text extracted with MuPDF, and the displayed definitions, Theorem 3, the full proof of properties (1)-(7) including the two-part Lemma for property (5), the proof of Bezout's theorem in §5.3 and Corollaries 1-3, and the §5.1-5.2 definitions inspected in the extracted text.

contents.name: §3.1 Multiple points and tangent lines: multiplicity from the lowest-degree term, tangent lines with multiplicity, node and ordinary multiple point, multiplicativity over components
§3.1 tangent lines and their multiplicities as factors of the lowest form
§3.2 Theorem 1: a simple point is exactly a point whose local ring is a DVR, with a uniformising parameter from a non-tangent line
§3.2 multiplicity one is equivalent to smoothness and the two definitions of tangent line agree at a simple point
§3.3 Theorem 3: existence and uniqueness of the intersection number, defined as dim_k O_P(A^2)/(F,G)
§3.3 property (1): the quotient is finite-dimensional exactly when the curves share no component through P
§3.3 properties (2)-(4) and (7): vanishing and locality, affine coordinate invariance, symmetry, and invariance under adding multiples
§3.3 property (6): additivity over products via the exact sequence 0 -> O/(F,H) -> O/(F,GH) -> O/(F,G) -> 0, with the cleared-denominator injectivity argument

§3.3 property (5): I(P,F∩G) >= m_P(F)m_P(G) with equality iff no common tangent, including Lemma (a) (containment of a power of the maximal ideal) and Lemma (b) (injectivity of the multiplication map)
§5.1 definitions of plane projective curves, degree, components, and multiple-component conventions
§5.2 linear systems of curves (the projective space of degree-d curves and its linear subspaces)
§5.3 Bezout's theorem: sum of intersection numbers equals the degree product for curves without a common component, proved by the graded exact sequence and Hilbert-function computation
§5.3 Corollary 1: sum of products of multiplicities is at most the degree product
§5.3 Corollary 2: if curves meet in exactly mn distinct points then all are simple on both
contents.reason: Follows immediately by combining the local inequality I_p >= m_p(F)m_p(G) with Bezout; the pair does not promise a separate simplicity criterion, and the companion's transverse examples already record the mechanism.

contents.name: §5.3 Corollary 3: two degree-m,n curves with more than mn common points share a component
§5.4 Multiple points: the bound on the sum of m_P(m_P-1)
contents.reason: Pluecker-adjacent arithmetic on the multiple-point count, excluded by the pair's stated boundary; the genus formula that consumes it returns after cohomology and adjunction on the later surfaces track.

contents.name: §5.5 Max Noether's fundamental theorem (AF+BG)
contents.reason: The AF+BG and adjoint-curve machinery is deliberately outside this pair's boundary; the pair proves Bezout and the local intersection calculus only, as the design's boundary paragraph requires.

contents.name: §5.6 Applications of Noether's theorem
contents.reason: Depends on the Noether AF+BG theorem excluded above; the companion builds its own worked incidence examples instead of importing the adjoint-curve applications.

contents.name: Problems 3.1-3.16 and 5.1-5.45
contents.reason: The problems develop practice computations, Pluecker-type formulas, and Noether applications; the companion page builds the pair's own worked examples, so no separate problem items are scaffolded.

sources.title: Michael Artin, MIT 18.721 Notes for a Course in Algebraic Geometry (January 26, 2022 version), Chapter 1: Plane Curves
sources.locator: Ch. 1 §§1.3-1.10, PDF pp. 9-35 (plane projective curves, tangent lines and flexes, resultants and discriminants, nodes and cusps, Bezout's theorem, Pluecker formulas)

read_evidence.method: Full 216-page PDF (4,590,458 bytes) downloaded from the MIT 18.721 course site, text extracted with MuPDF, and the statements of §§1.3-1.10 inspected in the extracted text, including Corollary 1.3.10 (multiplicity of a curve-line intersection), Proposition 1.3.12 (finitely many intersections), Definition 1.4.8 (ordinary flex), Proposition 1.6.10 and Lemma 1.6.21 (resultant degree and discriminant multiplicativity), Proposition 1.9.2 (Bezout for a line) and Proposition 1.9.3 (finiteness, bound and transversality).

contents.name: §1.3 Plane projective curves: degree, irreducible curves, intersection with a line as order of vanishing (Corollary 1.3.10), and finitely many intersections of coprime curves (Proposition 1.3.12)
§1.3 degree and component conventions for plane curves
§1.4 tangent lines, smooth points, flex points and ordinary flexes (Definition 1.4.8)
§1.4 tangency and smoothness of plane curves
§1.5 the dual curve and dual curve computations
contents.reason: Duality and the dual curve belong to the Pluecker-formula boundary expressly excluded from this pair; no dual-curve statement is promised or needed for Bezout.

contents.name: §1.6 resultants and discriminants: degree of the resultant (Proposition 1.6.10), discriminant multiplicativity (Lemma 1.6.21) and the elimination interface
§1.7 nodes and cusps: local models of the two classical singularities
§1.8 Hensel's lemma and local lifting of roots
contents.reason: The pair computes local intersection multiplicities by lengths and orders and never needs root lifting; Hensel machinery is not part of the promised claim scope.

contents.name: §1.9 Bezout's theorem: statement, the line case (Proposition 1.9.2), finiteness and the bound mn (Proposition 1.9.3(i)), and transversality (Proposition 1.9.3(ii))
§1.9 finiteness and the bound on the number of intersection points
§1.10 Pluecker formulas for smooth plane curves
contents.reason: Pluecker formulas are explicitly outside the pair's boundary; they need the dual curve and Hessian computations that this pair does not scaffold.

contents.name: §1.11 exercises
contents.reason: The exercises are computational drill and duality practice; the companion page builds its own worked examples from the scaffolded items instead of minting problem items.

read_evidence.method: Full 63-page consolidated PDF (863,420 bytes) downloaded from MIT OpenCourseWare, text extracted with MuPDF, and the complete relevant arguments of Lectures 15-16 inspected, including the tensor-length definition of mult_x(X,Y), the proof of Theorem 16.1, and Corollary 20.

contents.name: Lecture 15: divisors, linear equivalence, complete linear systems and the degree of a principal divisor (Definition 32, Proposition 25)
contents.reason: Divisors, linear equivalence and the Picard group on curves belong to the later Riemann-Roch material; this pair obtains its global degree identity from the published projective length formula instead.

contents.name: Lecture 16: definition of the intersection multiplicity of two plane curves as the length of the local tensor product i_*O_X tensor O_{P^2} j_*O_Y
Lecture 16 Theorem 16.1: Bezout's theorem, proved via the divisor of the section of O(d)
contents.reason: This is an independent cohomological proof of the same theorem the pair proves through the published projective length formula plus the local-to-global bridge; it needs divisor and line-bundle degree machinery deliberately not scaffolded here.

contents.name: Lecture 16 Corollary 20: the intersection multiplicity is greater than one at a non-smooth point of either curve
Lecture 16 smoothness and the m/m^2 embedding-dimension criterion (Definition 33, Example 25)
